title: Solomon's opening: all human affairs are empty
english: Thus says Solomon, son of David the king and prophet, the most honored king among all people and the wisest prophet, to the whole Church of God. How empty and useless are all human affairs and pursuits, everything that belongs to human life. For no one can point to any benefit attached to these things that people, crawling about the earth, are eager to accomplish with body and soul. They are defeated by temporal things, and they do not wish to see anything at all above the stars with the noble eye of the soul. Human life wears away day by day, through the cycles of hours and years and the fixed courses of the sun, as some things arrive and others slip away. The matter is like the passing of winter torrents that pour into the boundless deep of the sea with great turmoil. What God has established for human life remains fixed: being born from the earth, departing into the earth, the earth itself standing firm, the sun traveling around the whole earth and returning again to the same boundary, the winds likewise, and the rivers pouring into the sea—so many of them—and the winds that rush upon it, yet do not force it to overflow its limits, nor do they themselves transgress. These things that contribute to our life here have been fixed in this way. But the words and deeds devised by human beings have no measure. There is a great crowd of words, yet no benefit comes from this wandering idle talk. The human race is insatiable, both in speaking and in listening to another who speaks; and still more, it longs to gaze with careless eyes at everything that happens to come along. What could happen later that has not already been accomplished, or done by human beings? What new thing has not yet come to experience, that would be worth remembering? For I think there is nothing. Whatever someone might call recent or new, he will find upon reflection that it was not unknown even to the ancients. Just as former things are hidden in forgetfulness, so also present things will be dimmed in time for those who come after. And I am not improvising these things now as I address the Church; rather, having been entrusted with the kingdom of the Hebrews in Jerusalem, I have thought through all these things sufficiently.

title: Solomon recounts his exhaustive inquiry into earthly life and its futility
english: Solomon says: I searched carefully and understood wisely the whole nature of things on earth, and found it most varied. Human beings are given toil on earth, rolling about from one pretext of labor to another, ending in nothing. A strange and filthy spirit fills all things below, so that they cannot be recovered, nor even recalled to mind at all, such is the strangeness that has seized human affairs. For I once reasoned within myself, thinking I had become wiser than all who had come before me here; I came to know comparisons and the natures of things. I thought I was being carried along in vain on this course: knowledge follows wisdom, and toils follow knowledge.

translator_notes: The whole section paraphrases Ecclesiastes 1:13-18; citations are placed beside the clauses that render each verse. 'Spirit' (πνεῦμα) in 'a strange and foul spirit' renders Gregory's reading of the LXX 'choice of spirit' (προαίρεσις πνεύματος, Ecclesiastes 1:14) as an evil spirit; kept lower case. ἔγνων with the infinitive (συνεῖναι) is taken as 'I set my mind on / determined to' (compare Ecclesiastes 1:17 LXX 'I gave my heart to know'), not 'I learned to'. ἀναθυμηθῆναι is rendered 'reckon' (call to mind, count up), matching Ecclesiastes 1:15 'what is lacking cannot be numbered'. No doubtful readings in the copy-text.
orientation: Solomon describes his personal investigation of all activity under the sun, finding it wearisome, irrecoverable, and marked by a perverse spirit, concluding that wisdom brings knowledge but knowledge brings pain.

title: Testing pleasure and great works and finding them futile
english: Solomon continues: Convinced that things stood just so, I decided to turn to a different way of life. I would give myself to luxury and try pleasures of every kind. Now I see that all such things are futile altogether. I held back laughter when it ran loose, and I disciplined pleasure toward being self-controlled, rebuking it bitterly. I had reasoned that the soul can steady a bodily nature that gets drunk and flows like wine, and that self-control enslaves desire. So I became eager to see what earnest pursuit lies before people, and what truly good thing they will accomplish in this life.

I went through all the rest of the things people count admirable. I raised towering houses and planted vineyards, and I laid out gardens and acquired fruit trees of every kind and tended them (Ecclesiastes 2:4-6). There also I had great reservoirs built to hold water, set apart to water the plants abundantly. I surrounded myself with a crowd of household servants, menservants and maidservants, some bought from abroad and others born in my own house and raised there. Herds of four-footed animals came under my power, many cattle and many flocks, beyond anyone from earlier times. Treasures of gold and silver poured in to me, since I had made the kings of all nations my guards and tribute-bearers. Vast choirs were gathered for my delight, men and women together, performing a song in full harmony. For this side of luxury I appointed feasts and cupbearers, chosen from people of either sex, too many for me even to count; in these things I far surpassed those who had reigned in Jerusalem before me.

Then it came about that wisdom lessened in me, while desire for what was not good grew. I yielded to every lure of the eyes and to the unrestrained impulses of the heart that assailed me from all sides, and I gave myself over to hopes of pleasures. I bound my own choice to all those wretched luxuries. My thoughts were thus carried into misery, so that I judged these things good and judged that I ought to do them.

Then at last I came to myself and looked up. I saw that the things in my hands were troublesome and altogether hard, works of a spirit that was not good. For nothing chosen by people now appears to me acceptable and worth pursuing when judged by right reason.

translator_notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 2:1-11. 'Then it happened that my wisdom grew less' deliberately reverses Ecclesiastes 2:9b ('my wisdom remained with me'); Gregory reads Solomon's experiment as a fall, so that clause is left uncited to avoid presenting it as the verse's sense. The cupbearers 'from men and women alike' follow the LXX of 2:8 (οἰνοχόον καὶ οἰνοχόας). In 2:8 'the kings of all peoples' supplies 'peoples' for the bare genitive ἁπάντων ('of all'). 'Will' renders προαίρεσις (deliberate choice). 'A spirit that is not good' (πνεύματος οὐκ ἀγαθοῦ) again turns the LXX 'choice of spirit' (2:11) into an evil spirit; kept lower case. The choirs clause renders the men and women singers of 2:8 and is cited to that verse. No doubtful readings in the copy-text.
orientation: Solomon, as reported by Gregory, turns from searching wisdom to testing a life of luxury, pleasure and great building works.

title: Solomon weighs wisdom against folly, finds life in vanity grievous, and discerns the true good
english: Having reasoned through both the goods of wisdom and the evils of folly, I would rightly marvel at a person who is carried along unreasonably, then recovers himself and turns to what is proper. For the distance between prudence and folly is vast, the difference between them as great as day compared to night. The one who has chosen virtue resembles a man who sees each thing clearly and upward, his own course made in the season of brightest light; but the one entangled in vice, wandering in every kind of error as if in thick darkness, is blind in his outlook and cut off by the darkness of things. Finally, having devised the distinction between these two lives, I found nothing, and making myself a companion of fools I will receive the wages of folly. For what good is there from those sophistries, or what benefit from many words, when streams of idle talk surge forth as from a spring of folly? A wise person and a fool share nothing in common, neither according to human memory nor according to God's recompense. As for the affairs among humans, even while they seem to be just beginning, the end already seizes hold of them all. A wise person never shares the same end as one who lacks understanding. Therefore I hated even my whole life, the one consumed in empty things, which I passed burdened with toils upon the earth. For to put it concisely, everything has been painfully wrought for me as works of an unreasoning impulse; and someone else will inherit them, whether wise or foolish, reaping the cold fruits of my labors. Having received these things and cast them away, the truly good things set before a human being appeared to me: the knowledge of wisdom, and the possession of courage. But if someone has not attended to these, yet is infatuated with other things, such a person has chosen evils instead of goods, pursued vice instead of goodness, and toil instead of quiet, dragged along by varied disturbances, oppressed continually both night and day, by the body's pressing fatigue and the soul's unceasing anxieties, his heart fluttering because of alien matters. For the perfect good does not sit around eating and drinking; even if nourishment comes to humans especially from God, nothing of what is given to us for salvation lies outside his own providence. But the good man, obtaining wisdom from God, gains heavenly joy; whereas the wicked man, driven on by evils sent from God, sick with greed, strives to amass many things and hastens to insult the one honored by God before the Lord of all, offering useless gifts, making his own wretched pursuits both deceitful and empty.

translator_notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 2:12-26. Doubtful (flagged in the source row): the sentence ἔοικε ... βλέποντι· τῆς τε ἑαυτοῦ πορείας ... πεποιημένῳ is elliptical in both prints; read as 'like one who sees ... and who makes his journey in the brightest daylight'. ὑπὸ τοῦ σκότους τῶν πραγμάτων ἀφῃρημένος is read as 'cut off by the darkness from the things around him'; 'robbed by the darkness of affairs' is possible. τέλος in 'when I considered how the end of each of these two lives differs' is taken as a noun ('end, outcome', matching Ecclesiastes 2:14b-15), not as the adverb 'finally', which would contradict the day-and-night contrast just drawn. Variant not adopted: the Opera omnia print (zoomed image at D) appears to read εὗρον ὥσπερ (or ὅσπερ) οὐδέν ('I found it as nothing'); sense unchanged. Τέλος could also be the adverb 'in the end' ('in the end, when I considered the difference between these two lives, I found none'); the noun reading is kept because Gregory's answer echoes it (τοῦ αὐτοῦ κοινωνεῖ τέλους). Gregory then corrects the speaker's conclusion: 'the wise man and the fool have nothing in common' and 'the wise man never shares the same end' answer Ecclesiastes 2:16 ('how does the wise man die? Just like the fool'); the last two sentences of that paragraph are his comment and are not cited. The 'courage' (ἀνδρεία) of the goods set before a human being follows the LXX of 2:21 (ἐν ἀνδρείᾳ). 'For our preservation' renders πρὸς σωτηρίαν, since the context is food that keeps us alive; 'for our salvation' is the other possible sense. The perfect good 'does not rest in eating and drinking' denies the plain sense of 2:24 ('there is nothing better than to eat and drink'); the citation is kept because the clause visibly answers that verse and 2:24b-25 ('this also is from the hand of God'). 'Melting away over earthly toils' keeps the image of προστετηκώς (melted onto, clinging to); 'heart' is not in the Greek. 'The cheerless fruit' renders ψυχράς ('cold', i.e. joyless). 'Master of all' renders Δεσπότης and refers to God.
orientation: Solomon reflects on his own experience, comparing the man who chooses virtue with the man entangled in vice, and concludes that all his toil under the sun has been sorrowful and empty, so that the true goods set before humanity are knowledge of wisdom and possession of courage, which come from God.

title: Time full of opposites and the devil's war on God's creation
english: This present time overflows with every kind of opposite: births, then deaths; the sprouting of plants, then their uprooting; healings and killings; the building up of houses and their tearing down; weeping and laughter; mournings and dancings. Now someone gathers what comes from the earth, now he casts it out. At one moment he is mad for a woman, at the next he loathes her. Now he seeks something, now he loses it; now he guards it, now he squanders it; at one time he kills, at another he is killed; he speaks, then falls silent; he loves, then hates. For human affairs are at one time at war, at another at peace, as things that seem good veer sharply into acknowledged evils. Let us therefore cease from empty and useless toils. All these things, as it seems to me, were set in place to drive people mad with poisonous goads. A wicked opportunist has gaped around this age, straining to obliterate God's creation, having chosen from the beginning to war against it until the end. I am convinced that the greatest goods for a human being are cheerfulness and doing good, and that even this fleeting enjoyment comes from God only if righteousness leads his actions. As for the eternal and imperishable things that God has fixed firmly, nothing can be taken from them and nothing can be added. For anyone, then—yet so it is—those things are at once terrifying and wonderful. The things that have happened stand fixed; the things that will be have already come to pass through God's foreknowledge. And the one who is wronged has recourse to God as helper.

translator_notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 3:1-15. Doubtful reading (flagged in the source row, same words in both prints): ᾯ τινι οὖν, ἀλλ᾽ ἔστιν, ἐκεῖνα φοβερά τε ὁμοῦ καὶ θαυμαστά looks corrupt; 'To anyone at all' renders ᾯ τινι οὖν loosely, construed as the dative of ὁστισοῦν ('to anyone whatever'), and ἀλλ᾽ ἔστιν ('but it is') is given as 'Yet ... those things are'. Reviewer checked the Opera omnia zoom (z106c, at C): it reads Ὧι τινι οὖν, ἀλλ᾽ ἔστιν, as the copy-text. The Vossius Latin renders only 'Verum formidolosae simul et admirabiles illae sunt'. The sentence echoes Ecclesiastes 3:14b ('God has done it, so that people fear before Him') and is left uncited. 'What comes from the earth' (τὰ ἀπὸ γῆς) stands for the stones of 3:5; ἀποστυχεῖ is read as ἀποστυγεῖ ('loathes'). The tense shifts (present, then aorist) in the list of opposites are kept. 'A wicked one who watches for his chance' renders καιροσκόπος ... πονηρός; Gregory means the devil but does not name him, so neither does the English. 'What God has formed' renders τὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ πλάσμα (the creature God molded; compare Genesis 2:7, not cited as uncertain). The citation of 3:11 rests on the LXX wording αἰῶνα and ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς καὶ μέχρι τέλους, which Gregory turns into the devil's war on God's work. 'Has God for his helper' answers 3:15b ('God seeks what has been driven away').
orientation: Solomon continues his teaching, describing how the present age is filled with contrary events and how a wicked opportunist wars against God's creation, concluding that true good is cheerfulness and beneficence from God, while eternal things fixed by God cannot be altered.

title: Solomon sees the fate of the impious and pious below, and reflects on the equality of all before God
english: I saw in the lower regions a pit of punishment that receives the impious, while the pious have another place, untroubled. I considered that all things are reckoned alike by God and judged alike; the righteous and the wicked are the same, the rational and the irrational are the same. For the same span of time has been measured out for all, and death hangs over them; the kinds of beasts and of humans are the same in God’s sight, differing from each other only by the articulated voice. They experience everything in much the same way, and death comes no more upon the other animals than upon humans. For all have a similar spirit, and humans have no advantage over them, but all things are empty in a single word, having taken their composition from the same earth and having their dissolution into the same earth. For it is unclear concerning human souls whether they will fly upward, and concerning those of the irrational creatures whether they will flow downward. And it seemed to me that nothing else is good except enjoyment and the use of present things. For I did not think it possible to come again to the enjoyment of these, once a human being has tasted death.

translator_notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 3:16-22. Everything after the first sentence is in indirect speech governed by ἐλογισάμην ('I reasoned') and ᾠήθην ('I supposed'): it reports the speaker's former mistaken reasoning, not Gregory's settled view (he answers it in the next sections and in chapter 9). The English keeps that frame with 'I reasoned', 'I thought', 'I supposed' and past tense, and does not turn it into a plain statement. 'Breath' renders πνεῦμα, following the sense of Ecclesiastes 3:19 (πνεῦμα ἓν τοῖς πᾶσιν); 'spirit' is also possible. 'The regions below' (ἐν τοῖς κάτω μέρεσι) replaces the verse's 'under the sun'; Gregory reads the place of judgment as the underworld. καὶ ὅ μοι ἐδόκει at the start of the last paragraph is awkward Greek (ὅ without a clear antecedent); read as 'and so it seemed to me'. 'Pleasure' renders τρυφή (luxury, indulgence). The last sentence answers 3:22b ('who will bring him to see what will be after him?').
orientation: Solomon (reported) describes a vision of the underworld where the impious are received into a pit of punishment and the pious into a different, untroubled place, then reasons that God regards all alike — humans and animals share the same breath, death, and origin, and it is unclear whether human souls rise or animal souls descend.

title: On oppression, envy, and the solitary miser
english: Turning myself away from all these reflections, I looked closely; I turned away from every kind of false accusation that wanders among people. Some are wronged — they weep and lament, thrown down by force, with no one to defend them or comfort them at all, helplessness pressing on every side. Wrongdoers are lifted up to a height from which they will also fall. Of the wicked and the insolent, those who have died are better off than those still living. Better than both is the one who will be like them but has not yet come into being, because he has not yet touched the wickedness that belongs to human life. It also became clear to me how much envy follows a person from his neighbors — a goad of an evil spirit. The one who receives it, who takes it in and, as it were, clasps it to his breast, has nothing else but the consuming of his own soul, sawing and spending his own inconsolable grief along with his body, making the prosperity of others the cause of his grief. A sensible person would rather fill one hand with ease and meekness than both hands with toil and the cunning of a deceitful spirit. There is also something else I know that happens contrary to what is fitting, on account of a man's choice that is not good. He lives isolated on every side, having neither brother nor son, yet thriving in many possessions; he lives in insatiability, and he is unwilling to give himself over to any goodness at all. One would gladly ask him: for whose sake does such a man toil, fleeing the doing of anything good headlong, while he is torn apart by manifold desires to acquire wealth?

translator_notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 4:1-8. 'Oppression' renders συκοφαντίαι, following the LXX of 4:1 (συκοφαντίας), where the word means oppression and extortion, not only false accusation. 'Those who take the law into their own hands' renders χειροδίκαι (men of violence). Gregory limits 4:2 to 'the unjust and the reckless' (the dead have sinned less than the living); the English keeps that limit. 'More to be preferred' renders αἱρετώτερος. 4:5 ('the fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh') is turned into the envious man eating away his own soul; cited beside that clause. 'Will' renders προαίρεσις, as in section 2.1. ὅτου χάριν may be neuter ('for what reason') or masculine ('for whose sake'); 'for whose sake' follows Ecclesiastes 4:8 ('for whom do I toil?'). No doubtful readings in the copy-text.
orientation: Solomon reflects on human oppression, the folly of envy, and the misery of a man who has no kin yet hoards wealth, refusing himself any enjoyment.

title: Two together are helped, the lonely man is exposed
english: Far better than that solitary man are those who have made a partnership of life together, for they gather the finest fruit from it (Ecclesiastes 4:9). When two men devote themselves rightly to the same work, if anything happens to one of them, he has great help close by in the one who is with him (Ecclesiastes 4:10). For a man in trouble, the greatest misfortune is to be deserted with no one to raise him up.

Those who live together double their prosperity and comfort one another through the winter of unwelcome troubles. So by day they shine with open confidence in each other, and by night they rest in bright cheer. Whoever drags along an unshared life leads a dreadful life for himself without realizing it: if anyone sets upon people firmly bound together, he schemes boldly but unsafely, for a triple cord is not easily broken (Ecclesiastes 4:12). I myself prefer a poor young man who is wise to a foolish old king (Ecclesiastes 4:13) who has never taken to heart how it can happen that someone rises from prison to become king (Ecclesiastes 4:14), while the king himself justly falls afterward from his unjust rule.

Those who range themselves under the young yet sensible ruler, all who came before, live free from sorrow. But those who come later cannot praise even him, since they have no experience of any other ruler, but are led by thoughtless judgment and the impulse of a contrary spirit. And as you address the Church, keep before your eyes both to guide your own life rightly and to pray for the foolish, that they may gain understanding and learn to turn aside from the practice of evil.

translator_notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 4:9-16 and 5:1. Versification: the last sentence renders LXX/Hebrew Ecclesiastes 4:17, which is English Ecclesiastes 5:1; it is cited by the English number. The first sentence is printed with a question mark after τὰ βέλτιστα; a question introduced by a relative clause makes poor Greek, so it is rendered as a statement (sense unchanged). 'Winter' keeps χειμῶνα ('winter, storm'), which ties the image to the warmth of 4:11. 'A grim existence' renders φρικώδη ζωήν (a shuddering, dreadful life). 'Of sound mind' renders σώφρονα, where the verse has 'wise'. 'Those of the older generation' renders τοὺς ὅσοι προγενέστεροι; 4:15-16 is condensed by Gregory, and the clause is cited to 4:15. 'When you take part in the assembly' renders ἐκκλησιάζων (the verb Solomon used of himself in section 1); it answers 'when you go to the house of God' in the verse. The source row records one correction (ὅτι for ὄτι in the threefold-cord clause), already printed.
orientation: Gregory continues reporting Solomon's teaching, contrasting shared life with solitary toil and a foolish old king, and ends in his own voice addressing the Church.

title: Guarding speech and vows before God
english: It is good to spare the tongue and to use a steady heart when you apply yourself to words. For you must not, even if thoughts are irrational or out of place, let whatever comes to mind pour out through your voice. Instead, consider that even though we stand far from heaven, we speak to a God who hears, and it is profitable to speak without stumbling. Just as varied dreams follow the soul's many cares, so idle talk is joined to folly. A promise made in prayer should be fulfilled by action. It is the mark of fools to be worthless, but you be true, knowing it is far better not to vow at all, nor to pledge any deed, than to vow and then fail. You must in every way flee the influx of such fair-sounding words, since God hears. For the one who ponders this has nothing more than to perceive his own works being corrupted by God. For as many dreams are empty, so also many words. Fear of God is the salvation of humanity, yet it is rare. Therefore you must not wonder when you see the poor being oppressed and judges reasoning falsely. You must avoid seeming greater than those who are more powerful. For even if this comes about, wickedness itself will not rescue you from the terrors that will be yours.

translator_notes: Paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 5:2-9 in English numbering. Gregory's chapter 5 follows the LXX/Hebrew verse division, so LXX 5:1-8 = English 5:2-9; all citations use the English numbers. θεοῦ is lower case in the print at 'God will hear them' and 'destroyed by God' but plainly means God, so it is capitalised in English. οὐ in 'there is no need to wonder' is printed as text following the Opera omnia print (the transcription bracketed it as a supplement); the Latin 'nihil est cur mireris' agrees. In the dream comparison the Greek has two datives (φροντίσι ... φαντασίᾳ) with παρέπεται; read as 'dream images attend the cares of the soul'. κἂν ἄτοπα, ἢ τὰ ἐπὶ νοῦν ἐλθόντα is read as one idea, 'whatever comes into the mind, even when it is out of place'. 'Fine-sounding words' renders τῶνδε καλῶν ῥημάτων, taken as rash vows and boasts. 'Avoid seeming to be greater than those who are more powerful' takes τὸ ... δοκεῖν with the reader as subject; 'avoid thinking that the more powerful are greater' is a less likely reading. The last sentence ('your wickedness of itself will not rescue you') has no clear match in Ecclesiastes 5:9 ('the profit of the land is for all; the king is served by the field') and is left uncited.

title: The harm of greed and the good of enjoying one's labor as God's gift
english: Just as property taken by robbery is the most harmful and most impious thing a person can possess, so a man desirous of wealth never gets his fill, nor does he win the goodwill of those around him, even if he acquires a vast amount of silver. That is futile. Goodness, on the other hand, makes those who share in it exceedingly glad and produces brave men, giving them the power to look clearly at every circumstance. It is also a great thing to be free of such anxieties. For even a poor man, even if he is a slave and has not overfilled his own belly, enjoys the pleasant relief that comes through sleep. But the desire for wealth goes hand in hand with sleeplessness and toils of the soul. What could be more absurd than a man who, with great eagerness and care, hoards his wealth to preserve it, while keeping for himself the source of countless evils? That wealth must eventually be lost and destroyed, whether the owner has children or not. And even if he would not wish it, he himself must fall into the earth and depart, just as he was when he came into being. When he is about to leave with empty hands, he increases his own wickedness, as if forgetting that the end of his life lies upon him, similar to his birth, and that he toils uselessly, surrendering his whole life to the impulse of wind rather than to his own earnest effort, consuming it in utterly impious desires, in irrational impulses, and furthermore in sorrows and sicknesses. To sum up: for such a man his days are darkness, and his life is mourning. But that other thing is good and not to be thrown away: it is a gift of God for a human being to be able to enjoy his own labors with gladness, receiving God-given possessions, not ones taken by robbery. For that man is not sick with sorrows, nor is he, for the most part, enslaved to wicked thoughts; he measures out his own life with good deeds, remaining cheerful toward all, and exulting in the gift of God.

title: the misery of possessing everything yet enjoying nothing, and the folly of endless desire
english: I will set forth in the discourse the misery that most overwhelms human beings. God has fully supplied a man with everything his heart desires; nothing that enters his longing is taken from him — neither wealth, nor high reputation, nor any of the other things people are wildly excited about. He prospers in all things, as if gripped by this one god-sent evil alone: not enjoying them. He will lay it all up for his own companion, falling fruitless both for himself and for those near him. I offer this as a great sign and a clear demonstration of surpassing wickedness: a man called, unharmed, father of very many children, and who lives a long span of time, yet whose soul is not satisfied with goodness to such an extent, not even experiencing death — I would not envy him either for his multitude of children or for his multitude of days. And I prefer to him an untimely embryo fallen from the maternal womb. For just as it came in futility, so it departs in obscurity into oblivion, not having touched evils, nor having looked upon the sun. This is lighter than the lot of the wicked man, even if he measures out his own life for a thousand years and does not recognize goodness. Death is the end for both. The fool is convicted, above all by receiving no satisfaction of any desire. But the sober-minded man is not held fast by these passions. For the most part, an upright life leads a person into poverty. The sights that greedy eyes crave drive many out of their senses, stirring the soul and dragging it into useless pursuit through the empty desire to be seen. Now the things that have been born have already been known, and it is clear that a human being is not able to stand against those above him. Idle talks circulate among human beings, increasing the folly of those who use them.

title: Mourning and rebuke are better than laughter and songs
english: Knowing in advance the things pleasing to his heart that will meet him in life does the knower no good at all. Grant that for the sake of argument. Yet human meddling still contrives a further curiosity: to pry into what will come to each person after death and to claim to know it.

A good name delights the soul more than oil delights the body, and the end of life is better than its beginning (Ecclesiastes 7:1). It is better to mourn than to revel, and better to sit with those who grieve than with those who are drunk (Ecclesiastes 7:2). In this way, one who has reached the end of life has no anxiety about those around him. Thoughtful anger is better than laughter, for a stern face sets the soul straight (Ecclesiastes 7:3). The souls of the wise grow somber and restrained, while the souls of fools swell up and dissolve.

It is far more desirable to accept a rebuke from one wise man than to listen to a whole chorus of worthless and wretched men singing (Ecclesiastes 7:5). For the laughter of fools sounds like many thorns crackling in a fierce fire (Ecclesiastes 7:6). Slander is miserable as well, and indeed the greatest evil, for it plots against the souls of the wise and tries to corrupt the noble firm standing of good things (Ecclesiastes 7:7). One should praise the ceasing of words, not their beginning, and approve a measured temper, not one that is lofty and puffed up (Ecclesiastes 7:8). Above all, spare anger and do not rush headlong into rage, to which fools are enslaved (Ecclesiastes 7:9).

title: The superiority of wisdom over wealth and the danger of extremes
english: They are mistaken who say that life was better in former days, and they fail to understand how far wisdom surpasses a surplus of riches. It is as much more evident as silver appears brighter than its own shadow. For a human life is preserved not from acquiring perishable wealth, but from wisdom. Who, tell me, can recount fully the providence of God, so great and so kindly? Or who can call back the things that seem to have been neglected by God justly? Earlier, while acting wrongly, I observed everything: the just man holding to justice even to death, yet plotted against for it, and the godless man perishing in his own wickedness. A just man should not appear to be excessively so, nor excessively wise beyond measure, lest by some stumble he sin all the more greatly. And do not be reckless and headlong, lest untimely death seize you. The greatest good is to lay hold of God, and while doing so to commit no sin. For it is abominable to touch the pure with a defiled hand. But the one who yields with fear of God escapes every evil. Wisdom can do more to help than the support of the most powerful men in a city, and it justly makes allowance many times for those who fail in what is required. For not a single person is blameless. Nor should you pay any heed at all to the words of the godless, lest, hearing the words against you as a wicked slave's idle talk, then, stung at heart, you too turn in many deeds to curse back.

title: Solomon's loss of wisdom, entanglement with a deadly woman, and reflection on human perversity
english: I came to know all these things, having taken wisdom from God. Later I cast it away, and I was no longer capable of being like what I had been. For wisdom fled from me into an infinite length and into an immeasurable depth, so that it was no longer possible to grasp it. Consequently I completely ceased even from seeking it afterward. Nor did I any longer set my mind on understanding the follies and empty counsels of the godless, and a life that wanders. In such a disposition I was carried into those things, and being bound fast by a death-bearing desire, I knew the woman—some earth, or if anything else of such a kind existing. For her heart hunts with a dragnet those who pass by; but by merely joining hand to hand she holds a man as firmly as if she had wrapped him in bonds and dragged him off. One alone would be rescued from her, having God as propitious and overseeing; for the one who has been enslaved by sin would not escape. Seeking through all women their self-control, I found it in not one. And one might find a self-controlled man among a thousand, but not a woman. I considered this especially: that human beings, having become simple in souls by God, draw upon themselves varied reasonings and endless inquiries, and pretending to seek wisdom, they wear themselves out over little words.

title: Wisdom and the Fear of God Under a King's Authority
english: Wisdom is examined in a human being, and it shows through the face and gives light to the one who possesses it. Shamelessness, on the other hand, immediately shows the person in whom it dwells to be worthy of hatred, as soon as it is seen. You must pay careful attention to the words of the King. Flee every kind of oath, especially one that comes into God's name. Still, you ought to stand against an evil word, but guard yourself from all blasphemy against the Lord. For when the only Potentate and King brings something upon you, there will be no ground for complaint, and no one can speak against his decrees. It is better and more profitable to abide by the sacred commands and stay clear of evil words. A wise man knows and foresees the judgment that comes at the proper time, because that judgment will be just. All the affairs of human life await punishment from above. Yet the wicked man does not seem to know this very well. Even though great providence watches over him, nothing at all will escape notice in the time to come. He does not know what is coming, for no one will be able to announce any of it as it deserves. No one will be strong enough to prevent the angel who takes away his soul, and no method whatever will be found to evade the time of the end. Like a man caught in the middle of battle, destruction is inescapable from every side, and all human impiety is destroyed together.

title: Slow punishment emboldens sinners and people misjudge righteous and wicked
english: I am amazed whenever I look at the kinds of harm people devise against their neighbors, and how much of it. I know that the wicked are snatched away from here before their time and cleared out of the way, because they gave themselves over to emptiness.

God’s providence does not come swiftly upon everything, because He is greatly forbearing, and offenses are not punished at once (Ecclesiastes 8:11). For this reason the wicked man thinks he ought to go on sinning, as one who will escape unpunished. He does not understand that even when he has done wrong for a very long time, he will not escape notice. The greatest good is to fear God (Ecclesiastes 8:12). Once the impious man has fallen away from that fear, he will not indulge his own folly for long.

A worst and falsified opinion often spreads among people about the just and the unjust (Ecclesiastes 8:14). They assume the opposite about each sort. A man who is just is not thought to be so, while a man who is impious is thought wise. I count this delusion among the most grievous of all.

title: Testing pleasure as the greatest good
english: I once thought the greatest good was eating and drinking, and that the person most God-beloved was the one who enjoys these things throughout his life as much as possible. I considered cheerfulness of this sort the only consolation of life. So I gave my attention to nothing else but this notion, so that neither by night nor by day did I hold myself back from any of the pleasures people have devised. I came to know that no one indulging in these things will ever be able to find the true good, no matter how much he toils.

title: All share one end; the dead know nothing and have no further share
english: I used to suppose that all human beings at that time were deemed worthy of the same things. Even if someone was wise, cultivating righteousness and shunning injustice, and avoided hostility toward everyone by being upright — which is pleasing to God — that person appeared to toil in vain. One end seemed to belong to the righteous and the ungodly, the good and the bad, the clean and the unclean, and to the one who propitiates God and the one who does not. The unjust and the good, the perjurer and the one who altogether shuns oaths, were expected to be driven to the same end, and some judgment slips in that all will come to a similar end. I now recognize that these are the reasonings of the foolish, mere errors and deceptions. And they say many things: that the one who has died is gone completely, and that the living are preferable to the dead, even if the living lies in darkness or drags through life like a dog, rather than the dead lion. For the living at least know that they will die, but the dead know nothing. And no recompenses are laid up for them after they have paid the due. Both hatred and friendship toward the dead come to an end. For their zeal has ceased; their life has vanished. The one who has once departed from here has no share in anything.

title: Error still singing its counsel to indulge

Can you not see that God has given these things for enjoyment that is not hindered? (Ecclesiastes 9:7)"

"Put on freshly washed clothing, anoint your head with oil, look at this woman, and that one too, and vainly pass through this vain life. (Ecclesiastes 9:8; Ecclesiastes 9:9) For nothing else is left for you besides these things, neither here nor after death. So do whatever comes to hand. (Ecclesiastes 9:10)"

"For no one will exact an account of these things from you. What is done by human beings is not known at all outside human beings. And Hades, whatever it is, to which we are said to go, has no share in wisdom or perception. (Ecclesiastes 9:10)" That, on the one hand, is what the vain say.

translator_notes: Numbering is the same in English and LXX. Voice: everything inside the quotation marks is the speech of Error (ἡ πλάνη) personified, closed by 'That is what the vain say'; it is not Gregory's teaching (source row note). The claim that these things are 'given by God for enjoyment' belongs to Error's speech. The print sets a Greek question mark after βίον, closing a run of imperatives; the English treats them as commands. 'Look at this woman, and at that one' renders ὅρα τὴν γυναῖκα ταύτην, κἀκείνην δέ, Gregory's turn on LXX 9:9 'see life with the wife whom you love'. 'Whatever lies at hand' renders τὰ προστυχόντα, echoing 9:10 'whatever your hand finds to do'. 'My man' renders ὦ οὗτος ('you there'). Hades is kept as the Greek name of the underworld.
orientation: The voice of the foolish error is still speaking and urging indulgence before it is answered.

title: Wisdom surpasses strength and wealth; the poor wise man saves a city
english: But I know full well that even the swiftest runners will not finish that great race, and those who are powerful and fearsome, renowned among men, will not win the terrible war. (Ecclesiastes 9:11 LXX) Wisdom is not tested by an abundance of foods, and understanding does not usually share in wealth. I do not rejoice with those who think that all people will obtain like outcomes. They seem altogether to be sleeping, those who ponder such things and do not reckon that, like fish and birds snatched away, they will be worn down in evils, suddenly receiving their due penalty. (Ecclesiastes 9:12 LXX) I consider wisdom so great a thing that if a small city, inhabited by few men but besieged by the hand of a great king, possessed even one wise citizen who was poor, I would count that city great and mighty. (Ecclesiastes 9:13-14 LXX) For such a man could save his city both from the enemy and from the siege works. (Ecclesiastes 9:15 LXX) Yet others do not recognize that poor wise man; but I greatly prefer the strength that is in wisdom over this common force. (Ecclesiastes 9:16 LXX) Here wisdom is dishonored because it dwells with poverty; but later it will be heard speaking louder than rulers and tyrants who desire evil things. (Ecclesiastes 9:17 LXX) For wisdom is stronger even than iron; and the folly of one person works danger for many, even if that folly is despised by many. (Ecclesiastes 9:18 LXX)

translator_notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 9:11-18. 'That great race' keeps the demonstrative ἐκεῖνον; 'the fearful war' has none. 'Nor is prudence proved by a great deal of food' renders ἐν ἐδωδῆς πλήθει, Gregory's turn on 'bread to the wise' (Ecclesiastes 9:11). The sentence about those who think all meet the same lot recasts Ecclesiastes 9:11b ('time and chance happen to them all') by rejecting it; cited to that verse because it is Gregory's rendering of it. 'Others do not recognize' renders οὐ γινώσκουσι (Ecclesiastes 9:15 has 'no one remembered'). 'Its voice rising above' renders ὑπερφωνοῦσα (literally 'outshouting'). No Psalm citations, so no renumbering. 'I hold wisdom so great a thing' renders Ecclesiastes 9:13 ('this wisdom seemed great to me'), so that citation runs 9:13-15 (the 1622 Latin also starts verse 13 here). 'This common sort of power' renders ταύτης τῆς δημώδους δυνάμεως. 'Even if many despise it' takes folly (ἀφροσύνη) as the subject of κἂν ... ᾖ, as the 1622 Latin does ('etiamsi multis leuis & contemptibilis sit').
orientation: Gregory, speaking in his own voice, rejects the self-indulgent advice of the "vain ones" from the previous passage and asserts that true wisdom outweighs speed, power, feasting, and riches, illustrating this with a parable of a poor wise man who delivers a besieged city.

title: Flies in ointment; wisdom versus folly in leadership and danger
english: Flies fall into myrrh and suffocate there, spoiling both the look and the application of that sweet ointment. It is not fitting to remember wisdom and folly together in the same way. The wise person indeed guides himself toward the right in his dealings, but the fool has inclined toward the left, and he never takes folly as his guide to good deeds. The fool's thoughts are futile, stuffed full of folly. If a hostile spirit should ever fall upon you, my friend, stand firm, knowing that God is able to forgive even a multitude of many sins (Ecclesiastes 10:4 LXX). Such inversions are the works of a tyrant, and of the father of all wickedness: the fool is lifted high, while the rich person is humbled in prudence; slaves of sin are seen being carried on horseback, while holy men are seen walking on foot without honor, and the wicked exult (Ecclesiastes 10:5-7 LXX).

translator_notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 10:1-7. Reads ἐν ταὐτῷ (crasis of τῷ αὐτῷ) as corrected in the source row; rendered 'in the same breath'. χρίσις taken as the act or use of anointing, beside ὄψις 'look'. ἱλάσασθαι with God as subject rendered 'pardon' (the LXX sense of ἱλάσκομαι toward sins, God showing mercy), not 'atone for'; Ecclesiastes 10:4 has 'yielding pacifies great offences'. 'The father of all wickedness' is lowercased: it names the devil, not God; a possible echo of John 8:44 is left uncited. 'Tyrant' renders τυράννου, Gregory's reading of 'the ruler' in Ecclesiastes 10:5. No Psalm citations. 'He will use folly as a guide to good things' follows the 1622 Latin ('nec vnquam ad res praeclaras duce stultitia vtetur'); 'the man rich in prudence' likewise ('prudentiae ... opibus affluentem').
orientation: Solomon continues his teaching, using the image of flies spoiling ointment to illustrate how folly corrupts wisdom, then contrasting the wise who turn right with the foolish who turn left, and warning about a hostile spirit and the inversion of proper order under tyrants.

title: Treachery rebounds and foolish talk destroys
english: If someone plots against another, it escapes his notice that he is setting a snare for himself first and alone. The one who pulls down another's safety will fall foul of a serpent's bite. Moreover, the one who quarries stones will endure no small toil; and even the one splitting wood will carry the danger in his own tool. If the ax head should fly off the handle, the one doing this work will be thrown into confusion, since he gathers for no good purpose and only enlarges his own unjust and short-lived power. A serpent's bite is hidden; those chanting over it will comfort no one, for they are empty. But the good person works good for himself and for his neighbors, while the fool will fall into ruin through his own idle talk. And once he has opened his mouth, he begins foolishly and stops quickly, showing his folly all the way through.

translator_notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 10:8-14. Doubtful reading: MGR prints 'Ἀλλὰ μὴ [ἴσ. μὴν]'; read ἀλλὰ μήν with the editor's bracket and the 1622 Latin 'Quin is etiam', rendered 'Moreover'. 'He gathers to no good end, and he himself only increases his own unjust and short-lived power' follows Gregory's turn on the LXX of Ecclesiastes 10:10 ('he will strengthen his powers'); it is part of the same sentence as the axe and is left without a separate citation. 'Comes unseen' renders λαθραῖον (secret, stealthy). 'The good man does good both to himself and to his neighbors' stands where Ecclesiastes 10:12a speaks of the wise man's gracious words; cited with 10:12 as one verse. No Psalm citations. 'Leap from its handle' renders ἐκπηδῆσαι and avoids the English idiom 'fly off the handle'. 'The man at this work' matches the 1622 Latin ('qui huic operi incubit').
orientation: Solomon continues his teaching on the self-destructive nature of treachery and the ruinous character of idle talk, contrasting the good man's beneficial works with the fool's path to destruction.

title: Human inability to know and the contrast between good and bad rule
english: It is impossible for a human being to know anything, and to learn from a human being the things from the beginning or the things that are coming. For who will be the one to declare them? A human being who does not know how to go to the good city endures affliction, in his very eyes and in his whole face. I declare evils for that city whose king is young and whose rulers are gluttonous. But I call blessed the good land whose king is the son of the free man; there those deemed worthy to rule will enjoy good things in due season. The slothful and idle man, having become a mocker, diminishes a house; and driven by his own gluttony, using everything for it, led by silver, he endures doing all things shamefully and basely for a trifling price. It is fitting to obey a king, and rulers, and potentates, and not to make oneself hateful to them, nor to cast away any troublesome word toward them at all. For fear, lest the thing said in private somehow come into the open. For to the one king, rich and great, sharp and winged angels carry all things, rendering a service both spiritual and rational.

translator_notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 10:14-20. 'The good city' follows Gregory; the LXX of Ecclesiastes 10:15 has only 'the city'. 'The son of a free man' renders the singular ὁ τοῦ ἐλευθέρου υἱός (the LXX has 'son of free men'). In 10:18 the subjects are singular (ὀκνηρὸς καὶ ἀργός) with a plural verb and participles; rendered as a plural class ('the sluggish and the idle'). τὸ καὶ τὸ καταμόνας εἰρημένον is the idiom 'this or that said in private', rendered 'what is said even in private'. The last sentence turns 'a bird of the air will carry the voice' (Ecclesiastes 10:20) into angels serving God; 'the only King, rich and great' is capitalized because it names God. Possible echoes of 1 Timothy 6:15 ('the only Sovereign, King of kings') and Hebrews 1:14 (ministering spirits) are left uncited as uncertain. No Psalm citations. The opening binds τι to 'what was from the beginning or is to come', as the 1622 Latin does ('vt homo ea, quae a principio fuerunt, aut postea futura sunt, cognoscat'); it is not a claim that a human being can know nothing at all. 'Bring a house to decline' renders οἶκον ἐλαττοῦσι (diminish; Latin 'domum minuunt').
orientation: Solomon (reported) declares that humans cannot know past or future, laments a city under a young king and gluttonous rulers, praises a land ruled by a free man's son, condemns lazy officials who exploit everyone for money, and warns against cursing the powerful because angels serve the one great King.

title: Share bread and work without foreseeing the outcome
english: It is right to share bread and the necessities of life with others. Even if for the moment some think you are throwing it away, like entrusting bread to the water (Ecclesiastes 11:1), your love for mankind will not prove useless to you as time goes on. So give unsparingly and share what is yours with many, for you do not know what the coming day will bring (Ecclesiastes 11:2).

The clouds do not hold back their own heavy rain but pour the shower down upon the earth, and no tree stands forever: even if people spare it, the wind will still bring it down (Ecclesiastes 11:3). Many want to know beforehand what will come from heaven, yet the man who watches the clouds and waits for the wind held back from reaping or winnowing (Ecclesiastes 11:4), with nothing to convince him and no knowledge of what will come from God, just as he does not know what the pregnant woman will bear (Ecclesiastes 11:5).

Once you have sown in season, gather in the fruits whenever the time for that comes, for it is unclear which of the things that grow will turn out better (Ecclesiastes 11:6). May all things turn out for good.

translator_notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 11:1-6. 'Throwing it away' renders ἀπολλύναι (lose, destroy). 'Kindness' renders φιλανθρωπία (love toward human beings). 'What the coming day will bring about' renders the aorist ἐποίησεν with ἡ ἐπιοῦσα ἡμέρα as a gnomic future; cited to Ecclesiastes 11:2, whose second half it replaces. The wording is close to Proverbs 27:1 ('you do not know what a day may bring'), but that echo is uncertain and left uncited. 'Sure of nothing' renders ἐπὶ μηδενὶ πεπεισμένος. 'What kind of child' renders οἷον ('of what sort'); Ecclesiastes 11:5 speaks of the bones in the womb. The accented indefinite τὶ is read as 'anything'. No Psalm citations.
orientation: Solomon's teaching continues with commands about generosity and farming without knowing what will come from God.

title: The error of careless living before divine judgment
english: Someone reasoning might say the sun is beautiful, this life is sweet, and living long while rejoicing continuously is good. They might also say death is terrifying, an everlasting evil that brings one to nothing. Such a person thinks they ought to enjoy all present things that seem pleasant. They even advise the young to use their own time by releasing their souls into every pleasure, to indulge their desires, to do whatever seems right to them, to look at what delights them, and to turn away from what does not. To such a one I will say only this: you are senseless, O man, because you do not expect a judgment from God to follow all these things. But prodigality and licentiousness are evil, and the filthy, ruinous outrage against our bodies is destructive. For folly accompanies youth, and folly leads to destruction.

translator_notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 11:7-10. Voice: the first paragraph reports another man's reasoning and advice (λογιζόμενός τις ... οἴεται ... συμβουλεύει); it is not Solomon's counsel. Solomon answers from 'To him I will say'. ὦ οὗτος is a blunt address ('you there'). Ecclesiastes 11:9 is cited twice: once for the pleasure-seeker's advice, which restates the first half of the verse, and once for the judgment, which restates its second half. 'Abuse' renders ὕβρις (outrage, violation). No Psalm citations.
orientation: The author continues Solomon's voice, confronting a person who calculates that because the sun is beautiful, present life pleasant, and a long joyful life good, while death is dreadful and final, one should enjoy every present pleasure and advise youth to abandon themselves to desire — and warns that this reasoning forgets the coming judgment of God.

title: Call to fear God before the great day of judgment
english: One must still fear God while young, before handing oneself over to evils, before the great and terrible day of God arrives. On that day the sun will no longer shine, nor the moon, nor the other stars. The higher powers, the world-guarding angels, will be shaken in that universal winter and turmoil. Mighty men will cease their labors, and working women will cease as well, retreating into the dark recesses of their houses with all doors shut. A woman who has withdrawn from the grinding because of fear will use a voice as thin as the slenderest bird. All impure women will fall to the ground, and cities together with their blood-stained rulers will await punishment from above when the most bitter and bloody time comes, like a blossoming almond tree, and successive punishments press on like swarms of locusts descending. The lawless will be cast aside like a black and contemptible caper berry. The good man will go rejoicing to his eternal home, but the wicked, beating their breasts, will fill everything that is theirs, and neither stored-up silver nor tested gold will be of any further use. For a great blow will seize everything, as far as the water jar standing by a spring, and the cart-wheel left in the hollow, the time of its circuit having ceased, and life through water, once the laver-bearing age has passed. The only salvation for human beings lying on the earth is if their souls would come to know him and fly up to the one from whom they were also born.

translator_notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 12:1-7, read as the last day. Reads ἔτι and τὰ as corrected in the source row. Matthew 24:29 is cited beside the sun, moon and stars because Gregory joins the darkened lights to the shaking of the heavenly powers, as in that verse. 'The great and terrible day' also echoes Joel 2:31 and Malachi 4:5, but the Greek wording (φοβεράν) does not match the LXX (ἐπιφανῆ), so those are left uncited. 'The angels who guard the world' stands in apposition to 'the higher powers' and is Gregory's reading of 'the keepers of the house' (Ecclesiastes 12:3). 'Bloodstained governments' renders αἱ ἀρχαὶ αἱ μιαιφόνοι. 'Caper bush' renders κάππαρις (LXX Ecclesiastes 12:5). 'Beating of breasts' renders κοπτόμενοι (Ecclesiastes 12:5, the mourners). Doubtful: the sentence on the jar and the wheel is compressed. The English follows the print without emendation: χρόνον is the object of παροδεύσαντος in the genitive absolute ('when the age that brings the washing has passed beyond the time of the circling ... and of the life given through water'), as the 1622 Latin construes it ('ablutionem ferente seculo tum conuersionis atque iactationis, tum eius vitae quae per aquam comparatur, tempus praetergresso'). παυσαμένης (feminine genitive) is taken with περιδρομῆς ('the circling, now at an end'); the Latin passes over it. 'In the hollow' renders ἐν τῷ κοιλώματι; 'cistern' (LXX λάκκος) is not added. The 1622 Latin takes 'the age that brings the washing' (λουτροφόρου αἰῶνος) of baptism; the English keeps the literal image and does not add the word baptism. 'Begotten' keeps γεγέννηνται (have been begotten/born); Gregory's form of Ecclesiastes 12:7 (the spirit returns to God who gave it). No Psalm citations.
orientation: Solomon continues his address, urging the young to fear God before the terrifying day of the Lord arrives, describing cosmic upheaval, the collapse of human power, and the final separation of the good and the wicked.

title: Gregory's concluding confession of weariness and final admonition to fear God
english: Therefore I say again what I said before: human beings conduct themselves in utter futility, and there is no possibility at all that the futility of the things they devise could be exceeded. The toil is superfluous for me as I address the Church wisely, because I try to teach this people who are unteachably and incurably disposed. It takes a noble man to be able to understand words of wisdom. I am already an old man, and I have passed through a long span of life; I have toiled to discover the things pleasing to God through the mysteries of truth. I know that the commands of the wise rouse souls and sting no less than a goad drives bodies, or than bodies pierced by a nail. Some will hand on those wise teachings, having received them from one good shepherd and teacher, so that all of them in accord, as if from one mouth, narrate the things believed more abundantly. Many words bring no profit; nor do I advise you, friend, to write down useless things about what is fitting, in which toiling in vain is nothing more. But I shall need a conclusion something like this: O human beings, behold, I declare to you plainly and briefly: fear God, the master of all and overseer together; keep his commandments too; and be persuaded that everyone will afterward be judged, and each will receive the recompense of his own works according to their worth, both good and worthless together.

translator_notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 12:8-14, the end of the work. Reads ἃ (relative) as corrected in the source row. 'I am trying' supplies the finite verb missing in both prints after ὅτι διδάσκειν ἐπιχειρῶν. 'Preach wisely to the assembly' renders ἐκκλησιάζοντι, the verb behind the book's title (the Preacher). 'Could not be greater' renders 'admits no excess at all'. 'One good Shepherd and Teacher' is capitalized because, as in Ecclesiastes 12:11 ('one shepherd'), it names the divine source of the teaching; a possible echo of John 10:11 is left uncited. Doubtful: τὰ περὶ τὸ προσῆκον is unclear; it is rendered literally, 'about what is fitting'. Checked against the 1622 Latin (p. 96 A): it has 'ea, quae minus conueniunt' ('things that are less fitting'), as if reading παρά for περί; the English keeps the printed περί, and the doubt stays noted here. 'Good and bad alike' renders ἀγαθῶν τε ὁμοῦ καὶ φαύλων; the wording φαῦλος is close to 2 Corinthians 5:10, but that echo is left uncited as uncertain. No Psalm citations. 'Unteachable and past cure' renders ἀδιδάκτως καὶ ἀνιάτως ἔχοντα (Latin 'ut nec doctrinam nec curationem admittat'). 'Here I declare to you' renders ἰδοὺ ... προαγορεύω (Latin 'en vobis ... denuncio').
orientation: Gregory Thaumaturgus speaks in his own voice as an old man, reiterating the emptiness of human affairs, confessing the toil of teaching an unteachable people, and delivering a final charge to fear God and keep his commandments because all works will be judged.
